description: Paiyatuma, the Zuni Kachina of Dew and Dawn, is the flute-playing spirit who, in Zuni origin myths, brought the people the new music of his flute and led the seven Corn Maidens back to the pueblo after their wanderings. A patron of spring rains and the growing season, he is often cited as the model for the widespread Kokopelli Flute Player.
source: World History Encyclopedia (Paiyatuma, Joshua J. Mark, 2025); Bunzel, Zuni origin myths
research_notes: Verified via World History Encyclopedia article on Paiyatuma/Paiyatamu and Zuni origin myths. The input lists country as United States, which is correct for the Zuni of New Mexico. Also referenced the Kokopelli connection noted in Zuni scholarship.

description: Páutiwa is the winter-solstice kachina and the most venerable chief of the Zuni spirit pantheon. He rules Kothluwalawa, the spirit village beneath Kothluwalawa Lake, receives the spirits of the dead, and controls the ceremonial calendar, sending the kachinam to dance at Zuni when the world's rituals require them.
source: Tony Hillerman Portal, University of New Mexico (ehillerman.unm.edu)
research_notes: Verified via the Tony Hillerman Portal at the University of New Mexico. Páutiwa is the winter solstice kachina and chief of the spirit village beneath Kothluwalawa Lake. Country United States (Zuni, New Mexico) is correct.

description: Paiyatuma (Paiyatamu), the Zuni God of Dew and of the Dawn, is a flute-playing kachina celebrated in Zuni origin myths. He brought the Zuni the new music of the flute and presided over the Corn Maidens, and Zuni belief ties him to the life-giving moisture of morning and spring; scholars regard him as a probable prototype of the Pan-Southwestern Kokopelli Flute Player.
source: World History Encyclopedia (Paiyatuma, Joshua J. Mark, 2025); Zuni origin myth scholarship
research_notes: Same figure as paiyatuma-pueblo; this duplicate slug was retained because it appears in the dataset. Verified via World History Encyclopedia and Zuni origin myth scholarship. Noted as a probable model for the Kokopelli Flute Player.

description: Qalupalik (Qallupilluit) is a humanoid sea creature of Inuit tradition that dwells beneath Arctic shorelines and ice floes, waiting to snatch children who wander too close to the water. She carries her victims away in the hood of her amaut parka, and her eerie, ethereal humming lures the curious. The legend teaches children to keep away from dangerous sea ice.
source: Wikipedia 'Qallupilluit'; Inuit oral tradition sources
research_notes: Verified via the Wikipedia entry on Qallupilluit and related Inuit tradition sources. This is circumpolar Inuit lore. Country is listed as Canada, which is one of several valid regions for this being.

description: Qalupalik is the child-stealing ocean spirit told of across the Inuit world, including Greenland. She lives under the ice near the shore, rises silently through cracks to grab children playing alone on the floes, and tucks them into the pouch of her amaut parka. Her soft humming song is said to draw children toward the water's edge.
source: Wikipedia 'Qallupilluit'; Greenlandic Inuit folklore sources
research_notes: Greenlandic variant of the Qallupilluit/Qalupalik child-stealing sea spirit. Same tradition as qalupalik-inuit; distinct slug kept. Verified via Inuit folklore sources covering the circumpolar range including Greenland.

description: Qwaxw, the Raven of the Nuxalk people of Bella Coola, British Columbia, is the great transformer who freed the light: in the Nuxalk creation account of the four carpenters, Qwaxw released Nusximta, a crystal ball of sunlight held in a container, to light the world. His name echoes his call, and he stands at the center of Nuxalk origin stories.
source: Nuxalk Nation (nuxalknation.ca); The Tyee (2024) Nuxalk creation feature
research_notes: Verified via Nuxalk Nation cultural materials and a 2024 The Tyee article on Nuxalk creation. Tribe correction: the input lists country as United States, but the Nuxalk are a Nuxalkmc people of Bella Coola, British Columbia, Canada. Qwaxw means raven in Nuxalk and is named for its call.

description: Dzunuḵ̓wa (Tsonoqua, D'Sonoqua) is the Wild Woman of the Woods in Kwakwaka'wakw tradition: a naked ogress with pendulous breasts, tangled hair, and pursed red lips whose Hu! call rides the wind. She steals children in her basket, yet also brings wealth through her child, and her geekumhl mask appears at the close of the potlatch.
source: Wikipedia 'Dzunukwa'; Knowlton 1985 thesis on Kwakwaka'wakw ceremony
research_notes: Verified via the Wikipedia entry on Dzunukwa and Knowlton's 1985 thesis on Kwakwaka'wakw ceremony. Country listed as United States is wrong; the Kwakwaka'wakw are of coastal British Columbia, Canada. Dzunukwa is both feared child-stealer and bringer of wealth.

description: Haietlik, the lightning serpent of the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) peoples, is the great ally and weapon of Thunderbird in the whale hunt. Its head is sharp as a knife and its tongue flashes lightning that wounds whales for Thunderbird to take. Whalers carried its skin for luck, and its image appears on canoes and in petroglyphs.
source: Wikipedia 'Haietlik'; sacred-texts 'He'-e-tlik, The Lightning Snake'
research_notes: Verified via the Wikipedia entry on Haietlik and the sacred-texts account 'He'-e-tlik, The Lightning Snake.' The Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) of Vancouver Island, Canada are correctly listed as Canada. Allies of Thunderbird in whale hunts.

description: The Diyin Dine'é, or Holy People, are the supernaturals of Navajo tradition who shaped the world and gave the people ceremonies and lifeways. Chief among them is Changing Woman (Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé), who created the Navajo from her own skin and a bundle of mountain soil, instructing them to live in balance within the sacred landscape.
source: Wikipedia 'Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé'; Tony Hillerman Portal, University of New Mexico
research_notes: Verified via Wikipedia and the Tony Hillerman Portal at the University of New Mexico. The Diyin Dine'é are the Navajo Holy People; Changing Woman created the Navajo from her skin and mountain soil. Country United States is correct.

description: The Hero Twins of Navajo tradition are Monster Slayer (Nayénzgani) and Born of Water (Tobadzîschíni), twin sons of Changing Woman. They rid the world of the monsters that plagued it, journeyed to the house of their father the Sun, passed his trials, and returned armed with lightning. They remain the model of the Navajo warrior path.
source: Tony Hillerman Portal, University of New Mexico (ehillerman.unm.edu); navajopeople.org
research_notes: Verified via the Tony Hillerman Portal at the University of New Mexico and Navajo cultural sources. Monster Slayer and Born of Water are sons of Changing Woman who slew the monsters. Distinct from Killer-of-Enemies; these are brothers, not the same figure.

description: Hahai-i Wuhti is the Katsina Mother of Hopi tradition, mother of all katsinam, the spirit messengers who bring rain, gifts, and teachings to the people. Carved kachina dolls of her image have been collected at Oraibi on Third Mesa since the late nineteenth century, and she holds a central place in the Hopi ceremonial year.
source: Penn Museum; Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian kachina doll records
research_notes: Verified via Penn Museum and Smithsonian NMAI kachina doll records (Oraibi, Third Mesa) plus Hopi katsina literature. Hahai-i Wuhti is the Katsina Mother, mother of all katsinam. Country United States is correct.

description: In Jicarilla Apache creation accounts, Holy Boy is the restless spirit of the dark underworld who drove creation forward. When the Black Hactcin had shaped the animals and the world, Holy Boy grew weary of the darkness and pressed for the sun, moon, and light to be made, so that the people could live above in a bright world.
source: UTRGV Borderlands reader, Jicarilla Apache creation account (1930s oral tradition)
research_notes: Verified via the Jicarilla Apache creation account in the UTRGV Borderlands reader (1930s oral tradition). Holy Boy drives creation forward from the dark underworld alongside the Black Hactcin. Country United States is correct.

description: Hihaŋkaǧa, Owl-Maker, is an aged Lakota spirit who sits at the entrance to the Sky Road, the Milky Way, judging the naǧí, the souls of the dead. She admits only those whose bodies were properly tattooed; the rest she sends back to wander the earth as ghosts. She appears in Lakota lists of deities and accounts of the afterlife journey.
source: Wikipedia Lakota mythology; AAANativeArts
research_notes: Verified via the Wikipedia entry on Lakota mythology and AAANativeArts. Hihaŋkaǧa (Owl-Maker) judges souls at the entrance to the Milky Way. Country United States is correct.

description: Hahgwehdiyu, also called the Good Spirit or Good Mind, is the benevolent twin creator of Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) tradition, born normally to Sky Woman while his wicked brother Hahgwehdaetgah burst forth and killed her. He shaped the sky, made the sun from his mother's face, created the first people, and gave them corn, beans, squash, and tobacco.
source: Wikipedia 'Hahgwehdiyu'; native-languages.org Good Spirit and Sky-Holder pages
research_notes: Verified via the Wikipedia article on Hahgwehdiyu and native-languages.org. He is the Good Spirit (Good Mind), son of Sky Woman; his twin brother is Hahgwehdaetgah (Flint or Sawiskera). In some traditions he is identified with the high god Sky-Holder (Taronhiawagon). Country United States is correct.

description: Heloha, Thunder, and her mate Melatha, Lightning, are the two great birds of Choctaw tradition. The Sun Father sent them to warn the people of approaching storms. Heloha lays her enormous eggs on the clouds, where they roll about with a great rumble, while swift Melatha streaks across the sky leaving a trail of sparks. They are the comic pair of Choctaw storm myths.
source: Wikipedia Choctaw mythology; Halbert 19th-century Choctaw beliefs; Harrell, How Thunder and Lightning Came to Be
research_notes: Verified via the Wikipedia article on Choctaw mythology, Halbert's 19th-century collections of Choctaw beliefs, and the children's book 'How Thunder and Lightning Came to Be' (Harrell). Heloha (thunder) and Melatha (lightning) are two huge comic birds. Country United States is correct.

description: The Horned Serpent and the Tie-Snake (estakwvnayv) of the Muscogee Creek are underwater serpents of the Lower World, sometimes one creature and sometimes two, with the Horned Serpent the larger. It bears a great crystal on its forehead and crystalline scales prized for divination, its stag-like horns were used in medicine, and hunters who ate forbidden food could become such serpents.
source: Wikipedia 'Horned Serpent' and 'Muscogee mythology'; native-languages.org Tie-Snake; sacred-texts 'King of the Tie-Snakes'
research_notes: Verified via the Wikipedia entries on the Horned Serpent and Muscogee mythology, native-languages.org Tie-Snake, and the sacred-texts Creek tale 'King of the Tie-Snakes.' Estakwvnayv is the Muscogee term; Horned Serpent and Tie-Snake are sometimes identical, sometimes distinct. Country United States is correct.

description: No crane ghost is attested in Ojibwe tradition. In Anishinaabe culture the crane (Ajijaak, also Baswenaazhi, the Echo-Maker) is the leadership clan, one of the original seven doodemag, not a ghost or specter. This entry appears to be an AI template invention; the real crane figure is the clan totem that guided the Anishinaabe migration to Baawiting.
source: No attestation found in documented sources; entry appears AI-generated. Review of Anishinaabe clan and ethnographic materials.
research_notes: No attestation found in Ojibwe sources. Real basis: the Ajijaak (crane) doodem, one of the original seven Anishinaabe clans, which with the Loon Clan forms the hereditary leadership. Slug appears AI-generated.

The crane, Ajijaak, is the hereditary leadership clan, paired with the Loon Clan, and is celebrated for its loud voice at council rather than feared as a spirit. This entry appears to be an AI-generated invention with no basis in documented Anishinaabe folklore.

description: No giant crane appears in Ute folklore. Ute oral tradition centers on figures such as the trickster Sinawav (Coyote) and spirits of the mountains and waters, but a crane giant is unattested in the available ethnographic and linguistic sources. This entry appears to be a template-generated invention with no documented basis in Ute storytelling.
source: No attestation found in documented sources; entry appears AI-generated. Review of Ute ethnographic materials.

Documented Choctaw spirit beings include Kashehotapalo, Nalusa Falaya, Ishkitini, Okwa Nahola, and the thunderbirds Heloha and Melatha, but no crane guardian watches waters or guides fishermen in the recorded traditions. This entry appears to be an AI-generated invention.

description: No crane guardian spirit is attested in Hopi tradition. The historical Crane Clan (Atokngyam) once existed within the Snake phratry, but it is now extinct and held no guardian-deity role; no kachina of a crane guardian appears in the Hopi pantheon. This entry appears to derive only from the real but extinct clan name.
source: No attestation found in documented sources; entry appears AI-generated. Review of Hopi clan and katsina literature.
research_notes: The real Crane Clan (Atokngyam) existed in the Hopi Snake phratry but is extinct and was not a guardian spirit; the Crane and Eagle clans held the village-crier role and brought the Drab Flute and Maraú cults. No crane kachina guardian is attested. AI-generated from a real clan name.

description: No crane guardian spirit is attested in Lakota folklore. Lakota traditions honor Wakan Tanka, the Thunderbird (Wakinyan), and figures such as the owl spirit Hihaŋkaǧa, but cranes hold no recorded guardian role. Though cranes are good-luck omens among some peoples, a named Lakota crane guardian does not appear in the ethnographic record.
source: No attestation found in documented sources; entry appears AI-generated. Review of Lakota spiritual and ethnographic materials.
research_notes: No attestation found in Lakota sources. Cranes are good-luck omens in some tribes (native-languages.org crane legends page) but are not Lakota guardian spirits. AI-generated.

What is genuinely documented is the Crane Clan (Ajijaak or Baswenaazhi), one of the original seven doodemag and, with the Loon Clan, the hereditary leadership clan; white-crane chiefs met the first French explorers of Lake Superior. This entry inflates clan symbolism into an invented guardian figure.

No Passamaquoddy guardian spirit of this kind appears in the recorded ethnographic or oral sources.
